doc.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, November 11, 2017 [interview 2 of 2]

chapter: Lyrics and being in the moment
title: Writing lyrics to Think of One from a limousine job
summary: Gates explains his lyric approach and tells how a commuting Greenwich executive he drove inspired his lyrics to Monk's Think of One.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: So how does that song start for you when you work on your own tunes? Is there a—
Well Monk, the title. The title and the melody. So Monk called a tune “Think of One.”

So you can’t write lyrics to a song, a pre-established instrumental, without changing the title. Think of one. Too many things. So I was driving a limousine at the time, part time. And I would pick up this guy every Monday morning at 5 a.m. in Greenwich, Connecticut. Greenwich, Connecticut is the Hollywood Hills of Connecticut. Beautiful big English Tudor, a Bentley parked in the driveway, maybe a German sports car. This is early 90s. Swimming pool, tennis courts, gated driveway. I’d pick this guy up, nice guy. Get in the car he’d sleep. I’d take him to the London airport — er, I’d take him to JFK but I’d take him to London Air. He’d get on the plane, go there. I would pick him up Thursday night at midnight and bring him back to Greenwich and drop him off. And he’d sleep in the car. I did that for, I don’t know, two months. I mean I was driving for a car service, a limousine service, and this was part, one of the jobs that I did. Nice guy, didn’t talk much because he was tired. He was shot. Air travel back and forth to London every week. Of course I only picked him up and brought him back and forth. One time I picked up his wife, she was flying somewhere. And another time I picked up their Au Pair. She was going back to Scandinavia, to Sweden. And I never — of course I wasn’t around for this but I never saw him driving the Bentley or the Porsche. I never saw him playing tennis. I never saw him in the swimming pool. One two three four five six seven. How many things do you need? Eight nine ten or eleven. Is it just greed? That’s where those lyrics came from. Because he’s working so hard to have all of this he never got to use any of it. Maybe his wife did occasionally. Who knows? I don’t know. I’m going to say something that’s way out of whack that’s supposed to be funny: maybe she was busy

with the pool boy. I don’t know. But he couldn’t take care of anything because he was busy making money. Well how much money do you need? How much do you need? How about honing in on one thing. At least in that moment in time that’s the way I felt. Now I wish I had the English Tudor and the Bentley. No not really.
I bet you’d make use of it.
